hero.title: Price Elasticity of Demand — Why Petrol Prices Never Stop Traffic
hero.hook: Petrol prices double — traffic barely drops. Phone prices drop 20% — sales explode. The same price change, completely different results. Why? The answer is one of the most exam-tested ideas in Economics.

hook_section.scenario: In 2022, petrol prices jumped 40% across India. Did people stop commuting? Barely. But when a popular phone brand runs a 20% sale, it sells out in minutes. Why does the same percentage change produce such different buying behaviour?
hook_section.bridge: It comes down to whether a good has substitutes, whether it's a necessity, and what share of income it takes. Economists measure this sensitivity with one number — the Price Elasticity of Demand.
hook_section.punchline: Elasticity tells you HOW MUCH quantity responds to a price change — not just whether it does.

concept_section.analogy: Think of demand as a rubber band. Some goods (luxuries, things with many substitutes) stretch a lot — a small price rise sends buyers running. Other goods (petrol, medicines, salt) barely stretch — buyers need them regardless. Elasticity measures how stretchy the band is.
concept_section.principle: PED = % Change in Quantity Demanded ÷ % Change in Price. If |PED| > 1 → Elastic. If |PED| < 1 → Inelastic. If |PED| = 1 → Unitary elastic.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each type to understand it 👇

reveals.question: 🔴 Perfectly Inelastic (PED = 0)?
reveals.answer: Quantity doesn't change at all with price. Example: insulin for a diabetic patient — price irrelevant, they must buy it. Vertical demand curve.

reveals.question: 🟡 Inelastic (0 < PED < 1)?
reveals.answer: Quantity changes less than price. Example: petrol, salt, medicines. People buy almost the same amount even if price rises.

reveals.question: 🟢 Elastic (PED > 1)?
reveals.answer: Quantity changes more than price. Example: branded clothing, restaurant meals, luxury gadgets. A small price drop causes a big jump in sales.

reveals.question: 🔵 Perfectly Elastic (PED = ∞)?
reveals.answer: Any price rise causes demand to drop to zero. Example: a firm in perfect competition — consumers switch to identical competitors instantly. Horizontal demand curve.

points: Necessities are inelastic (petrol, rice, medicines); luxuries are elastic (cars, holidays)
More substitutes → more elastic (branded tea vs generic tea)
Proportion of income: expensive items (TV) → more elastic than cheap items (salt)
Time period: demand is more elastic in the long run (time to find substitutes)
Revenue rule: elastic demand → lower price increases revenue; inelastic → higher price increases revenue

quiz.q: If price of a good rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 15%, PED is:
quiz.exp: PED = % ΔQd / % ΔP = −15/10 = −1.5. Magnitude is 1.5 > 1, so demand is elastic.

quiz.q: Which of the following goods is likely to have inelastic demand?
quiz.exp: Life-saving medicines are necessities with no substitutes — people buy them regardless of price, making demand highly inelastic.

quiz.q: A perfectly elastic demand curve is:
quiz.exp: PED = ∞ means any price change causes infinite change in quantity. The demand curve is horizontal — consumers buy any quantity at exactly one price.

quiz.q: If a firm lowers price and total revenue increases, demand is:
quiz.exp: With elastic demand (PED > 1), a price cut causes a proportionally larger rise in quantity, so total revenue (P×Q) increases.

flipcards.front: Formula for Price Elasticity of Demand?
flipcards.back: PED = % Change in Quantity Demanded / % Change in Price
Elastic demand — quantity responds more than price change (luxuries, substitutes)
Inelastic demand — quantity barely responds (necessities, no substitutes)

flipcards.front: What type of curve has PED = 0?
flipcards.back: Perfectly inelastic — vertical demand curve. Same quantity regardless of price.

flipcards.front: Effect on revenue when price drops and demand is elastic?
flipcards.back: Total revenue increases — quantity rises by more than price falls

flipcards.front: Why is demand for salt inelastic?
flipcards.back: Salt is a necessity with no substitutes and takes a tiny share of income
